4. **Master kill switch + protected domains**: Where exactly is `cold_email_sending_enabled` checked in the real send path (already confirmed `true` in the prod Settings table)? Where is the protected-domains check (`cold_email_protected_domains` setting) implemented, what are the DEFAULT protected domains if the setting is empty/unset (cite the literal default list/logic), and does it reference `APP_URL`'s host automatically? 

   Extra context you don't need to re-derive: prod DB currently has exactly ONE `SendingDomain` row — `trynxeon.com` under Brand "Nxeon" (`physicalPostalAddress` = "4157 Verte Place, Nanaimo, BC, V9T 5P7, Canada", already filled in), with ONE `Inbox` — `hello@trynxeon.com`, status ACTIVE, dailyCap 40, currentRampCap 40 (fully ramped), warmupDay 30, minGapSeconds 100. Given that, tell me plainly based on the actual code: was `trynxeon.com` clearly set up as a deliberately-isolated cold-sending domain specifically so bulk cold email never touches the primary `nxeon.cloud` domain's reputation? Does the protected-domains code make it hard/impossible to register `nxeon.cloud` itself as a cold-email `SendingDomain` (e.g. would it fail a compliance/readiness check, or is there no actual code-level block, just a practice)?

5. **Dry-run/preview capability**: Is there a genuine existing function/server-action anywhere in `lib/actions-coldemail.ts`, `sender.ts`, or `compliance.ts` that renders the EXACT final subject/HTML a send would go out with (post-merge-fields, post-footer-injection, post-tracking-pixel/link-injection) WITHOUT creating a real `ColdSend` row or calling the mail transport? Cite it exactly (function name, file:line). If nothing like this genuinely exists, say so clearly — don't stretch a partial match into a "yes."

Keep the report under 2000 words, structured by question number, always with file:line citations. If something is genuinely ambiguous or not found after a real search, say so explicitly rather than inferring.

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.

})
<commentary>
The agent starts with no context from this conversation, so the prompt briefs it: what to assess, the relevant background, and what form the answer should take.
</commentary>
</example>

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. The one exception is a workshop document from the `workshop` skill, which carries its own design: there Claude skips `artifact-design` and loads `artifact-diagramming` for a template page's diagrams. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com or cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ (the skill has the full list) and stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data or images) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, at most 255 entries and 64MB per version, and standard web media types only.

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

)"

- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

6307	## Cold Email Engine — OVERHAUL Phase 1: the Reply Loop + Master Inbox (2026-08-11)
6308	
6309	Turns the send-only engine into a **two-way platform**. Before this, the engine was *deaf*: it sent
6310	sequences but never read a reply, so its hero KPI (reply / positive-reply rate) was structurally always
6311	zero, follow-ups couldn't stop on a mail-side reply, and there was no operator workspace between launches.
6312	This phase adds an **IMAP reply poller**, a **conversation store**, a **unified Master Inbox (unibox)**, an
6313	**AI reply classifier**, and **outbound webhooks**. Built on branch `feature/coldemail-overhaul-inbox`.
6314	Additive to Phase 1/2/3 — no existing model/enum value changed.
6315	
6316	**Safety posture.** The bulk kill-switch `cold_email_sending_enabled` stays **off** — bulk campaigns still
6317	don't fire. IMAP polling + reply-send are **inert until an inbox has real credentials** (a blank `imapHost`/
6318	`smtpHost` is never contacted). A 1:1 operator reply to someone who already replied is *normal* email and
6319	may send from that inbox's SMTP even while the bulk switch is off — it never touches the bulk queue. Every
6320	credential + webhook secret is stored **encrypted** via `lib/crypto-box` (write-only in the UI, never logged,
6321	never echoed back). The whole reply loop is demoable on a **single real mailbox** without enabling bulk send.

# Cold Email Engine — Code Audit (read-only, /opt/nxeon)

## 1. Compliance footer injection

**Automatic — not something a campaign author has to add.** The footer is injected unconditionally inside `buildMessage()`:

- `lib/coldemail/sender.ts:250-254` — `complianceFooter(identity, unsubscribeUrl)` builds the plain-text footer and `renderFooterHtml()` builds the HTML block; both are concatenated into `contentHtml` regardless of any options:
```
const footerText = complianceFooter(identity, unsubscribeUrl);
...
let contentHtml = `${bodyHtml}\n${footerHtml}`;
```
- `renderFooterHtml` itself: `lib/coldemail/sender.ts:286-294`.
- The only thing gated by an option is *tracking* injection (`opts.track`), at `sender.ts:255-260` — the footer is not behind that flag.

**The one real call site in the bulk send path** is `worker/coldemail.ts:416-424`, inside `processDueSends`, immediately before `transport.send(msg)`:
```
const msg = buildMessage({ identity: sendIdentity, step: s.step, contact: s.contact, sendId: s.id, base: linkBase, footerDisclosure: ctx.footerDisclosure, track: true });
```
There is no other call to `buildMessage` in the send loop, and no branch that reaches `transport.send`/`chosen.smtp` without going through it first (`worker/coldemail.ts:361-497` is one linear per-row loop). So for **bulk campaign sends** there is no skip flag or early-return that bypasses footer injection.

**However, there is a second, separate real send path that bypasses `buildMessage` entirely and carries no footer/unsubscribe link:** `sendConversationReply()` in `lib/coldemail/inbox-send.ts:34-103`. It hand-builds its own `RenderedMessage` (lines 81-88: `from/to/subject/html/text/headers` with no compliance footer, no `List-Unsubscribe` header, no unsubscribe link) and sends it via `NxeonSmtpTransport` directly (lines 90-98). Per its own header comment (lines 1-9), this is the "1:1 operator reply" feature — replying inside an existing `Conversation` thread — deliberately allowed to run even while the bulk kill-switch is off. It is a real, reachable code path (`app/admin/coldemail/inbox` → `sendReply` action) where an email to a real recipient goes out with **no** CAN-SPAM footer or unsubscribe link, by design (framed in-code as ordinary correspondence, not bulk outreach).

## 2. Unsubscribe mechanism

- **Token**: `unsubscribeToken(contactId, brandId)` — `lib/coldemail/compliance.ts:113-117`, format `v1.<base64url(contactId:brandId)>.<hmac-sha256(AUTH_SECRET)>`; verified constant-time by `verifyUnsubscribeToken` (`compliance.ts:126-151`).
- **Route**: `app/api/coldemail/unsubscribe/route.ts`. `GET` (lines 123-129) only renders a confirm page (no state change, to avoid mail-client link-prefetch triggering it). `POST` (lines 131-148) calls `applyUnsubscribe()` (lines 97-121).
- **Suppression row written**: `applyUnsubscribe` writes `scope: "GLOBAL"`, `reason: "UNSUBSCRIBE"` (route.ts:116-118) — **always GLOBAL**, never brand-scoped, and idempotent (only inserts if no existing GLOBAL row for that email, lines 111-119). The same GLOBAL scope is used by the separate hygiene sweep for bounces/complaints (`worker/coldemail-deliverability.ts:263-267`).
- **RFC 8058 headers**: set in `buildMessage()`, `sender.ts:265-272`:
```
"List-Unsubscribe": `<${unsubscribeUrl}>`,
"List-Unsubscribe-Post": "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click",
```
Confirmed only present when a message goes through `buildMessage` — the `sendConversationReply` path (Q1) does not set these headers.

## 3. Pacing / rate-limiting — real numbers

Two distinct systems exist:

**A. Per-inbox warmup ramp (Phase 3, the one actually driving real bulk sends).** Presets in `lib/coldemail/warmup.ts:36-41`:
| Preset | start→target/day | ramp days |
|---|---|---|
| CONSERVATIVE | 5 → 30 | 28 |
| STANDARD | 5 → 40 | 21 |
| AGGRESSIVE | 10 → 50 | 14 |
| ADAPTIVE | 5 → 40 | 21 (same as STANDARD, plus health back-off) |

Ramp is linear via `warmupDailyLimit()` (`warmup.ts:85-92`), clamped by the inbox's `dailyCap` in `inboxAllowedVolume()` (`warmup.ts:131-138`). Schema defaults (`prisma/schema.prisma:4568-4582`): `dailyCap` default **40**, `startCap` default **5**, `targetCap` default **40**, `rampDays` default **21**, `minGapSeconds` default **100** ("90–120s between sends reads human", schema comment). `saveInbox` (`lib/actions-coldemail.ts:1229-1252`) defaults new inboxes to the STANDARD preset unless overridden. This exactly matches the prod inbox you cited (dailyCap 40, currentRampCap 40, warmupDay 30, minGapSeconds 100 — fully ramped STANDARD).

**B. Brand-level flat cap (Phase 2, `effectiveDailyCap`, `compliance.ts:36-37,241,266-287`).** `DEFAULT_DAILY_CAP = 40`, `WARMUP_STEP = 5` (day1=5, +5/day). This is still computed in `processDueSends` (`worker/coldemail.ts:302-315`) but only used as an early-exit gate `if (!useRotation && sentToday >= cap) return 0` — and since the fallback send path was intentionally removed (comment at `worker/coldemail.ts:386-398`: "There used to be a Phase-2 fallback here... that path is exactly what an audit found still silently defeating the isolation fix"), **any brand with inboxes registered sends exclusively through the rotation/warmup system (A)**, not this flat cap.

**`selectNextInbox`** (`rotation.ts:85-95`): filters to inboxes passing `isInboxEligible` (`rotation.ts:65-76` — status ACTIVE or WARMING, `authGreen` true, `remainingCapacity()>0`, and `minGapSeconds` elapsed since `lastSendAt`), then sorts **oldest-`lastSendAt`-first (LRU)**, tie-broken by **most remaining capacity**. It is cap-gated and auth-gated as part of eligibility, and LRU for ordering.

**Where pacing is actually enforced — both, but differently:**
- **At schedule time**: `scheduleCampaignSends()` (`worker/coldemail.ts:217-272`) sets each `ColdSend.scheduledFor` by cumulative `SequenceStep.delayDays` from `campaign.launchedAt` (lines 225-231) — this spaces *sequence steps* across days, but every contact's step-1 row typically gets the *same* `scheduledFor`, so a whole list can become "due" simultaneously.
- **At send time**: the worker then throttles the actually-due backlog: a `MAX_SENDS_PER_SWEEP = 50` budget (`worker/coldemail.ts:154`), jittered `sleep()` between sends (`THROTTLE_MIN_MS=800`/`THROTTLE_MAX_MS=2600`, lines 156-160, applied at line 497), and — critically — `selectNextInbox` returning `null`/`break` (line 400) the moment no inbox has remaining ramp capacity or has cleared its `minGapSeconds`, leaving the rest `QUEUED` for a later sweep. So real daily-volume pacing is enforced by the **worker's per-sweep inbox-capacity gating**, not by spreading `scheduledFor` across days.

## 4. Master kill switch + protected domains

- **Kill switch**: `worker/coldemail.ts:517` — `if (!(await getSettingBool("cold_email_sending_enabled", false))) return;` — line one of `coldEmailSendSweep()`, before any DB query.
- **Protected-domains check**: built by `protectedDomainSet(configured, appHost)` (`compliance.ts:356-367`) and applied via `isProtectedDomain()` (`compliance.ts:373-382`) inside `evaluateSendEligibility()` (`compliance.ts:397-441`). Called from the worker at `worker/coldemail.ts:539,561` (guardrails #2/#3, per-campaign, every sweep) and from the admin `launchCampaign` action via `brandEligibility()` (`lib/actions-coldemail.ts:704-707`).
- **Default protected domains** if the setting is empty: `ALWAYS_PROTECTED_DOMAINS: readonly string[] = ["nxeon.cloud", "mail.nxeon.cloud"]` (`compliance.ts:339`), always merged in code regardless of the Setting value — `protectedDomainSet` unions this base set with `appHost` and the operator-configured list (`compliance.ts:358-364`), so clearing the setting can never expose these two. Matching also blocks **any subdomain** of a protected apex (`isProtectedDomain`, `compliance.ts:378-379`), and an empty/unresolved domain is treated as protected — "refuse, never fail open" (`compliance.ts:375`).
- **Yes, it references `APP_URL`'s host automatically**: `appHost()` is defined identically in both `worker/coldemail.ts:162-168` and `lib/actions-coldemail.ts:695-701`, reading `new URL(process.env.APP_URL).host`, and is passed as the second argument to `protectedDomainSet` at both real call sites (`worker/coldemail.ts:539`, `actions-coldemail.ts:705`).

**Is `trynxeon.com` deliberately isolated?** Yes, and the code enforces it structurally, not just by convention: `evaluateSendEligibility` requires a *dedicated, non-protected* sending domain (`compliance.ts:409-437`, checks `dedicatedDomain` + `notProtected`), and the worker's rotation-pool loader explicitly refuses to ever fall back to the shared platform SMTP transport for cold mail (`worker/coldemail.ts:386-398`, with an incident writeup in the comment about an earlier bug that broke this isolation). `trynxeon.com` passing that gate while `nxeon.cloud`/`mail.nxeon.cloud` are hardcoded-protected is exactly what makes the isolation real in code, not just practice.

**Can `nxeon.cloud` itself be registered as a `SendingDomain`?** At the **DB-write level, yes — nothing stops it.** `saveSendingDomain()` (`lib/actions-coldemail.ts:981-1009`) does no protected-domain or eligibility check at all before `db.sendingDomain.create(...)` (line 1000); it only validates the domain regex (line 991) and that the brand exists. The block only bites **later**, at send-eligibility evaluation: `evaluateSendEligibility` would return `eligible: false` with reason `Sending domain "nxeon.cloud" is a protected platform domain — cold email must use a dedicated domain` (`compliance.ts:429-433`, exercised by `test/coldemail-sender.test.ts:80-87`), which blocks it at **Launch** (`launchCampaign`, `actions-coldemail.ts:704-714` onward) and again every sweep (`worker/coldemail.ts:561-569`, logged as `coldemail.send.brand_blocked`). So: registerable, but structurally unable to ever send — it would fail the compliance/readiness check every single time, both at launch and at every sweep, forever.

## 5. Dry-run/preview capability

**A true pre-send message-content preview does not exist.** The only "preview" function is `previewCampaign(campaignId)` — `lib/actions-coldemail.ts:607-684` — and it is a **recipient-count dry-run only**: it counts `suppressed` / `dead` / `alreadyEmailed` / `missingConsent` / `sendable` against the list (lines 650-672) and returns a `CampaignPreview` object (lines 588-599). It never calls `buildMessage`, never renders a subject/HTML/merge-fields/footer/tracking, and does not touch `ColdSend`.

Confirmed by a full-repo search: `buildMessage` (the only function that produces the exact final subject/HTML, post-merge-fields, post-footer, post-tracking) is called from exactly one place outside its own test file — `worker/coldemail.ts:416`, inside the real send loop. There is no server action, route, or admin-UI code path anywhere in `lib/actions-coldemail.ts`, `sender.ts`, or `compliance.ts` that invokes `buildMessage` for preview purposes. So: **no, nothing genuinely renders the exact outgoing message without a real send** — `previewCampaign` is a partial match (recipient math, gated by the same `requireBrandCompliance`) but not a content preview, and should not be represented as one.
